subject: literature
title: The Brontës and the Victorian Woman's Novel, c. 1840–1880: pen names, governesses and the fight to be taken seriously
dek: In the middle of the nineteenth century, three sisters from a Yorkshire parsonage, a Manchester minister's wife and a translator who called herself George Eliot turned the English novel into the place where women's inner lives, anger, work and marriages were examined in public. They did it while the law still treated a married woman as part of her husband.
era: c. 1840–1880, from the Brontë sisters' first publications in 1846–47 to the death of George Eliot in 1880, with roots in Wollstonecraft and Austen and an afterlife in the New Woman novel, Virginia Woolf and feminist criticism.
honesty: This lesson keeps to facts documented in the English Wikipedia articles on the Brontë family, Charlotte, Emily and Anne Brontë, Jane Eyre, Wuthering Heights, The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, Elizabeth Gaskell, George Eliot, Middlemarch, the Matrimonial Causes Act 1857, the Married Women's Property Acts, the Langham Place group, sensation novels and Kate Bush, plus the quotations as they appear in those sources. Quotations from letters are given as they are commonly quoted; small differences in punctuation exist between editions. It is text only today, with no images.

timeline.label: Wollstonecraft's Vindication
timeline.detail: Mary Wollstonecraft publishes A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, arguing that women seem less rational only because they are denied education.

timeline.label: Jane Austen's novels
timeline.detail: Austen publishes Sense and Sensibility, Pride and Prejudice, Emma and others anonymously ('By a Lady'). She dies in 1817.

timeline.label: The Brontës move to Haworth
timeline.detail: Patrick Brontë, an Irish-born clergyman, becomes perpetual curate of Haworth in West Yorkshire. His wife Maria dies the next year.

timeline.label: Two eldest sisters die
timeline.detail: Maria and Elizabeth Brontë fall ill at the Clergy Daughters' School at Cowan Bridge and die. Charlotte later uses the school as the model for Lowood in Jane Eyre.

timeline.label: Southey's letter
timeline.detail: Charlotte sends poems to the Poet Laureate Robert Southey, who replies that 'Literature cannot be the business of a woman's life, and it ought not to be.' Victoria becomes queen the same year.

timeline.label: Poems by Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell
timeline.detail: The sisters pay to publish a joint book of poems under male-sounding pen names. It famously sells only two copies in its first year.

timeline.label: Jane Eyre, Wuthering Heights, Agnes Grey
timeline.detail: Jane Eyre comes out in October from Smith, Elder and is an immediate success. Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey follow in December from Thomas Cautley Newby.

timeline.label: Tenant of Wildfell Hall; Mary Barton
timeline.detail: Anne's novel about a wife who leaves an alcoholic husband sells well. Elizabeth Gaskell publishes Mary Barton about Manchester workers. Branwell and Emily Brontë die.

timeline.label: Anne dies; Shirley
timeline.detail: Anne dies at Scarborough in May. Charlotte, the last surviving sibling, publishes Shirley.

timeline.label: Villette, Charlotte's death, Gaskell's Life
timeline.detail: Charlotte publishes Villette (1853), marries Arthur Bell Nicholls (1854) and dies in March 1855. Gaskell's Life of Charlotte Brontë appears in 1857.

timeline.label: Matrimonial Causes Act
timeline.detail: Divorce moves from Parliament to a new civil court, but a husband can divorce for adultery alone while a wife must prove adultery plus another offence.

timeline.label: Adam Bede
timeline.detail: Mary Ann Evans, writing as George Eliot, has her first big success. Readers speculate about who George Eliot is.

timeline.label: Sensation novels
timeline.detail: Ellen Wood's East Lynne (1861) and Mary Elizabeth Braddon's Lady Audley's Secret (1862) become best-sellers about secrets, bigamy and crime inside respectable homes.

timeline.label: Middlemarch
timeline.detail: George Eliot's novel of a provincial town is published in eight parts.

timeline.label: Married Women's Property Acts
timeline.detail: The 1870 Act lets married women keep their own earnings; the 1882 Act lets them own and control property in their own right.

timeline.label: George Eliot dies
timeline.detail: She dies in December, months after marrying John Cross.

fun_fact.title: Kate Bush and Emily Brontë share a birthday
fun_fact.text: Kate Bush wrote 'Wuthering Heights' at 18, after seeing the last minutes of a television adaptation, and sang it in the voice of Cathy's ghost at Heathcliff's window. Released in 1978, it went to number one in the UK for four weeks and made her the first woman to top the UK chart with a song she had written herself. She was born on 30 July 1958; Emily Brontë was born on 30 July 1818, exactly 140 years earlier.

sections.title: Wollstonecraft, Austen and a law that erased wives

blocks.text: To understand why the Brontës and George Eliot mattered, start with the legal position of a woman in early Victorian England. Under the common-law doctrine of coverture, a married woman had no separate legal identity. Her property, her earnings and, until the Custody of Infants Act of 1839, her children belonged to her husband. Divorce required a private Act of Parliament and was almost impossible for a wife to obtain. Middle-class women were expected to marry; if they did not, one of the few respectable jobs open to them was to become a governess, living in another family's house, neither servant nor equal.

Two earlier writers framed the problem. Mary Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) argued that women appeared weak and frivolous because they were trained to be ornaments rather than educated to think. Jane Austen, publishing anonymously between 1811 and 1817, wrote comedies of courtship in which money and marriage decide a woman's whole future. Her heroines are witty and clear-eyed, but her novels mostly stay in the drawing room and end at the wedding.

The novel itself was growing fast. Circulating libraries such as Charles Edward Mudie's, founded in 1842, bought novels in expensive three-volume editions and rented them to middle-class subscribers, which made the novel a family product that had to be fit for daughters to read. Women had always written novels, but critics often treated 'lady novelists' as producers of light entertainment. This is the world into which three sisters from Yorkshire sent their manuscripts under men's names.

sections.title: Haworth: six children, invented kingdoms and a parsonage by the moors

blocks.text: Patrick Brontë was born in Ireland to a poor family, studied at Cambridge and became a Church of England clergyman. In 1820 he took the post at Haworth, a hill village above the wool towns of West Yorkshire, with the moors behind the parsonage and the graveyard in front. His wife Maria died in 1821, leaving six children. In 1824 the four eldest girls were sent to the Clergy Daughters' School at Cowan Bridge, where conditions were harsh; Maria and Elizabeth fell ill and died in 1825. Charlotte, Emily, Anne and their brother Branwell grew up at home, largely educated by their father and by their own reading.

In 1826 Patrick brought Branwell a box of toy soldiers, and the children began writing stories about them. Charlotte and Branwell built an imaginary African kingdom called Angria; Emily and Anne broke away to create Gondal, an island realm. They wrote in tiny hand-made books in minute script, producing a huge body of juvenilia. This private apprenticeship lasted into their twenties and taught them to write romance, politics and violence long before anyone outside the house read a word.

As adults the sisters worked as teachers and governesses, and hated it. Charlotte and Emily went to Brussels in 1842 to study at the Pensionnat Heger, hoping to open their own school; Charlotte went back alone in 1843 and fell painfully in love with her married teacher, Constantin Heger. The school plan failed. Branwell, meant to be the family genius, lost a tutoring post in 1845 after an affair with his employer's wife and sank into drink and opium.

In 1845 Charlotte found Emily's poems and pushed the sisters to publish. Poems by Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell appeared in 1846 at their own expense. They chose names that kept their initials but were, as Charlotte later explained, ambiguous, because they had noticed that critics judged women authors with prejudice. The book sold two copies. They kept going, each writing a novel.

sections.title: Jane Eyre: 'I am no bird; and no net ensnares me'

blocks.text: Jane Eyre: An Autobiography, 'edited by Currer Bell', was published by Smith, Elder in October 1847 and was a success within weeks. It follows an orphan from an abusive childhood with her aunt, through the starving charity school of Lowood, to a job as governess at Thornfield Hall, where she falls in love with her employer, Edward Rochester. On their wedding day she learns that he already has a wife, Bertha Mason, a Creole woman from Jamaica who is locked in the attic and described as mad. Jane refuses to become his mistress, leaves with nothing, nearly dies on the moors, and returns only when she is independent, with an inheritance, and he is widowed and injured.

What startled readers was the first-person voice. Jane is poor, plain and small, and she insists that she has the same soul and the same feelings as anyone. 'Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and little, I am soulless and heartless?' she tells Rochester. Elsewhere she says: 'I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will.' The novel also contains a famous passage in which Jane, pacing the roof at Thornfield, reflects that women feel just as men feel and suffer from too rigid a restraint. The ending's line, 'Reader, I married him,' is the most quoted sentence in the book, and notably Jane is the subject of the verb.

Not everyone approved. In 1848 the critic Elizabeth Rigby, in the Quarterly Review, called the book anti-Christian and said its tone was the same one that had 'fostered Chartism and rebellion at home'. Much later, critics turned to Bertha. Jean Rhys's novel Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) tells Bertha's story from her side, as a Caribbean woman renamed and imprisoned by an English husband, and Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar's study The Madwoman in the Attic (1979) read her as the angry double that Victorian women writers had to hide.

sections.title: Wuthering Heights and The Tenant of Wildfell Hall

blocks.text: Emily's Wuthering Heights, published by Thomas Cautley Newby in December 1847 together with Anne's Agnes Grey, is a very different book. It is told at second and third hand, mainly by a visiting tenant, Mr Lockwood, and the housekeeper Nelly Dean, and it follows two families on the moors across two generations. At its centre are Catherine Earnshaw and Heathcliff, a foundling of unknown origin taken in by her father. Catherine marries the gentle Edgar Linton for status while declaring of Heathcliff, 'I am Heathcliff.' Heathcliff's revenge against both families fills the rest of the book. Early reviewers found it brutal and confusing; in Taiwan it is usually known as 咆哮山莊. Emily wrote no other novel. She caught a cold at Branwell's funeral in September 1848, refused medical help for weeks and died in December, aged 30.

Anne, the youngest, is often treated as the quiet sister, but her second novel was the most openly political. The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848) is about Helen Graham, who leaves her alcoholic, abusive husband Arthur Huntingdon and lives under a false name with her young son, supporting herself by painting. At the time a wife who left her husband had no legal right to her child or her earnings, so Helen's escape is in fact illegal. The novel sold well, and when critics called it coarse Anne answered in a preface to the second edition that she wished to tell the truth and that she could not see why a woman should be condemned for writing what would be proper for a man. Anne died of tuberculosis at Scarborough in May 1849, aged 29. After her death Charlotte prevented a reissue of Tenant, which partly explains why it was neglected for so long.

Agnes Grey, Anne's first novel, is a calm, precise account of a governess mistreated by her employers' children and ignored by their parents. Read beside Jane Eyre, it shows the same job without the romance.

sections.title: Charlotte alone: Shirley, Villette and the biography

blocks.text: Within nine months, from September 1848 to May 1849, Charlotte lost Branwell, Emily and Anne. She finished Shirley (1849), a novel set during the Luddite machine-breaking of 1811–12 that includes frank passages about the emptiness of life for unmarried middle-class women. In 1848 she and Anne had travelled to London to prove to Smith, Elder that the Bells were separate people, and Charlotte now entered literary society, meeting Thackeray and becoming friends with Elizabeth Gaskell.

Villette (1853) returns to Brussels. Its narrator, Lucy Snowe, is a lonely English teacher in a foreign school who hides her feelings even from the reader, and many critics consider it Charlotte's most mature book. In 1854 she married her father's curate, Arthur Bell Nicholls, and she died in March 1855, aged 38 and pregnant; the cause is debated between tuberculosis and severe pregnancy sickness. Her first novel, The Professor, was published after her death in 1857.

Patrick Brontë asked Gaskell to write his daughter's life. The Life of Charlotte Brontë (1857) is one of the most famous English biographies and created the image of the three sisters as isolated geniuses on the wild moors. It also caused a scandal: Gaskell's account of Cowan Bridge and of the woman blamed for Branwell's ruin led to threats of a libel action, and passages had to be withdrawn.

sections.title: Elizabeth Gaskell: factory towns and women's work

blocks.text: Elizabeth Gaskell (1810–1865) was married to William Gaskell, a Unitarian minister in Manchester, the world's first great industrial city. Her first novel, Mary Barton (1848), published anonymously, describes the hunger of cotton workers during the depression of the early 1840s and the murder of a mill-owner's son, and it angered some manufacturers by taking the workers' side. North and South (1854–55), serialised in Charles Dickens's magazine Household Words, follows Margaret Hale, a clergyman's daughter from the south, who argues with a northern mill-owner, John Thornton, about strikes and responsibility while falling in love with him.

Gaskell also wrote Cranford (serialised 1851–53), a gentle comedy about a small town run almost entirely by single women and widows, and Ruth (1853), which shocked readers by making an unmarried mother its sympathetic heroine. Some families burned the book. Her last novel, Wives and Daughters, was unfinished when she died suddenly in 1865.

sections.title: George Eliot: the most learned woman in England writes under a man's name

blocks.text: Mary Ann Evans (1819–1880) grew up in Warwickshire, the daughter of an estate manager. As a young woman she lost her evangelical faith, which caused a long quarrel with her father. She translated David Friedrich Strauss's The Life of Jesus from German (1846), moved to London and became, in practice, the editor of the radical Westminster Review in the early 1850s, though her name did not appear. In 1854 she began living with the writer George Henry Lewes, who was married and could not obtain a divorce, because he had accepted his wife's children by another man as his own. Respectable society shunned her for years.

In 1856 she published an essay in the Westminster Review called 'Silly Novels by Lady Novelists', mocking fiction in which brilliant, beautiful heroines dazzle everyone. Her complaint was not that women wrote novels, but that bad ones gave critics an excuse to dismiss all women. When she began writing fiction herself she chose the pen name George Eliot, partly to be judged seriously and partly to protect her work from the scandal of her private life. Scenes of Clerical Life (1857–58) was followed by Adam Bede (1859), a great success. A man named Joseph Liggins was even put forward as the real author, which helped push her identity into the open.

Then came The Mill on the Floss (1860), about Maggie Tulliver, a passionate, clever girl whose education is sacrificed to her brother's; Silas Marner (1861); Romola (1862–63), set in Renaissance Florence; and Middlemarch (1871–72). Middlemarch, subtitled 'A Study of Provincial Life', follows a whole Midlands town around 1830, but its central figure is Dorothea Brooke, a young woman who wants to do something great and makes a disastrous marriage to the dry scholar Edward Casaubon. Eliot ends by saying that Dorothea's influence on those around her was 'incalculably diffusive', and that 'the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts', owed to those 'who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs.' Virginia Woolf later called Middlemarch 'one of the few English novels written for grown-up people.'

Her last novel, Daniel Deronda (1876), took up Jewish identity and early Zionism, unusual for an English novel of the time. Lewes died in 1878. In May 1880 she married John Walter Cross, a man twenty years younger, and she died that December. Because of her irregular life she was refused burial in Westminster Abbey and lies in Highgate Cemetery beside Lewes; a memorial stone was placed in Poets' Corner only in 1980.

sections.title: Poets, sensation novelists and the Langham Place women

blocks.text: Women's writing in these decades was broader than the three great names. Elizabeth Barrett Browning's verse novel Aurora Leigh (1856) follows a woman poet who refuses a marriage proposal in order to pursue her art. Christina Rossetti's Goblin Market (1862) is a strange, sensual poem about two sisters and the fruit sold by goblin men. Harriet Martineau, a journalist and economist, wrote best-selling popular explanations of political economy and an autobiography published after her death.

In the 1860s a new genre called sensation fiction filled Mudie's shelves. Ellen Wood's East Lynne (1861) and Mary Elizabeth Braddon's Lady Audley's Secret (1862), together with Wilkie Collins's The Woman in White (1859–60), told stories of bigamy, poison, false identities and madhouses inside respectable middle-class homes. Critics worried that such books, many written by women, were corrupting young female readers, and the very anxiety shows how much the domestic novel had become a space for questioning marriage.

At the same time, organised feminism took shape. In 1856 Barbara Leigh Smith (later Bodichon) organised a large petition for married women's property reform, and in 1858 she and Bessie Rayner Parkes founded the English Woman's Journal, around which the Langham Place group gathered. Bodichon helped found Girton College for women at Cambridge in 1869; George Eliot was a friend and a donor. John Stuart Mill presented a women's suffrage petition to Parliament in 1866 and published The Subjection of Women in 1869. The Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882 finally allowed married women to keep their earnings and then their property. The novels did not cause these laws, but they made the problems they addressed vivid to a large reading public.

sections.title: What else was happening in the world at the same time

blocks.text: In 1848, the year of Tenant and Mary Barton, revolutions broke out across Europe, Marx and Engels published The Communist Manifesto, and in the United States about 300 people met at Seneca Falls, New York, where Elizabeth Cady Stanton's Declaration of Sentiments demanded rights for women, including the vote. In America, Margaret Fuller had published Woman in the Nineteenth Century in 1845, Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) became the best-selling novel of the century, and Emily Dickinson was writing nearly 1,800 poems in Amherst, almost none published in her lifetime.

In France, Aurore Dupin, writing as George Sand, had already scandalised readers from the 1830s with novels such as Indiana (1832) about unhappy marriages and with her habit of wearing men's clothes; George Eliot admired her. Flaubert's Madame Bovary (1857), about a provincial wife destroyed by romantic dreams and debt, appeared the same year as Britain's Matrimonial Causes Act. In Russia, the realist novelists covered in an earlier lesson were writing about the 'woman question' too, from Chernyshevsky's What Is to Be Done? (1863) to Tolstoy's Anna Karenina (1875–77).

In East Asia, the same decades saw the Opium Wars and the Taiping Rebellion in China and the opening and Meiji Restoration of Japan, covered in history lessons on this site. Taiwan was a Qing frontier prefecture; ports such as Tamsui were opened to foreign trade around 1860 under treaties that followed the Second Opium War. Women's novels in Chinese or Japanese on the Victorian model would come later: in Japan, Higuchi Ichiyō wrote her short stories in the 1890s, and the Seitō women of 1911 were explicitly reading Western women writers.

sections.title: New Women, Woolf and the madwoman in the attic

blocks.text: In the 1880s and 1890s a wave of 'New Woman' fiction argued openly for women's education, work and sexual freedom. Olive Schreiner's The Story of an African Farm (1883), published under the name Ralph Iron, and Sarah Grand's The Heavenly Twins (1893) were best-sellers, and Thomas Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891) and Jude the Obscure (1895) carried similar questions. By then women no longer needed male pen names to be read seriously, though many still used them.

Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own (1929) is partly a response to this generation. She praised Austen and Emily Brontë for writing without bitterness, argued that Charlotte's anger at her confinement sometimes broke into her novels, and imagined how much more these women could have done with money and a room of their own. In the 1970s feminist critics, notably Elaine Showalter in A Literature of Their Own (1977) and Gilbert and Gubar in The Madwoman in the Attic (1979), made the Brontës and Eliot central to the study of a women's literary tradition.

The novels have never left popular culture. Jane Eyre and Wuthering Heights have been filmed dozens of times; the Brontë Parsonage at Haworth has been a museum since 1928; and Chinese-speaking readers have known them for a century as 簡愛 and 咆哮山莊 (in mainland China 呼嘯山莊).

items: The Victorian women's novel turned a woman's private feelings, especially anger and desire, into a serious subject, told in her own voice.
Pen names were a strategy, not modesty: the Brontës and George Eliot hid their sex so that their work would be judged on its merits.
The plots follow the law closely. Governess jobs, trapped wives, lost children and property explain why so many of these heroines have so few choices.
These novels did not pass laws, but they built a large reading public that could imagine a wife leaving a husband or a single woman working, which helped reform campaigns such as Langham Place.
Later readers, from Jean Rhys to Gilbert and Gubar, showed that the same books also contain blind spots, especially about empire and race, as in the figure of Bertha Mason.

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: Helen Graham in The Tenant of Wildfell Hall breaks the law simply by leaving a violent husband with her child and earning her own money. Taiwan's domestic violence and protection-order laws now exist because of organisations like the ones you are studying for cool dairy. Which parts of Helen's situation have been solved by law, and which parts, such as money, housing and social shame, still depend on support services and donors today?
